content: Patients with diabetes mellitus often use complementary and alternative medications, including Ayurvedic treatments. It is therefore essential to evaluate the efficacy and safety of these interventions. This review aimed to assess the effects of Ayurvedic treatments for diabetes mellitus. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, AMED, and others, up to October 2011. Hand searches of journals and reference lists of potentially relevant trials were also performed. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials lasting at least two months, involving participants of any age, gender, or type of diabetes, regardless of disease duration, comorbidities, or complications. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the risk of bias in the included studies, following the guidelines outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. However, due to the heterogeneity of interventions and variability in data quality, only a limited number of studies could be combined for analysis. Seven studies were included, involving a total of 354 participants (172 in the treatment groups, 158 in the control groups, and 24 with unclear allocation). The treatment duration ranged from three to six months, and all studies focused on adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Six trials investigated proprietary herbal mixtures, while one trial examined a whole-system Ayurvedic treatment. For primary outcomes, significant reductions in glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c), fasting blood sugar (FBS), or both were observed with the use of Diabecon, Inolter, and Cogent DB compared to placebo or no additional treatment. However, no significant hypoglycemic effects were noted with Pancreas Tonic or Hyponidd. The study on whole-system Ayurvedic treatment did not provide data on HbA1c or FBS. One study on Pancreas Tonic found no significant improvement in health-related quality of life. Adverse effects were minimal. One study reported drug hypersensitivity in a single patient in the treatment group. Another study noted one hypoglycemic episode in the treatment group, though no severe hypoglycemia occurred. Gastrointestinal side effects were reported in one study, affecting one participant in the intervention group and none in the control group. None of the studies reported deaths, renal toxicity, hematological toxicity, or liver toxicity. For secondary outcomes, postprandial blood sugar (PPBS) levels were lower in participants treated with Diabecon, unchanged with Hyponidd, and higher in those treated with Cogent DB. Lipid profiles were not significantly affected by Pancreas Tonic or Hyponidd. However, Inolter treatment resulted in higher HDL cholesterol, lower LDL cholesterol, and reduced triglycerides. Cogent DB treatment was associated with lower total cholesterol and triglycerides. Diabecon treatment was linked to increased fasting insulin levels, and one study also reported higher stimulated insulin and fasting C-peptide levels. No significant changes in fasting or stimulated C-peptide and insulin levels were observed with Hyponidd, Cogent DB, or Pancreas Tonic. The study on Inolter did not assess these outcomes. None of the included studies investigated diabetic complications, mortality, or economic outcomes. In conclusion, while some herbal mixtures demonstrated significant glucose-lowering effects, the methodological limitations and small sample sizes of the included studies prevent definitive conclusions about their efficacy. Although no significant adverse events were reported, the current evidence is insufficient to recommend these interventions for routine clinical practice. Further well-designed studies are necessary to establish their safety and efficacy.
